name: Frances 'Frankie' Lowry
languages: Polish (her grandmother's kitchen, enough to be fed and scolded)
equipment: Heavy coat: a man's grey ulster bought secondhand on Smithfield Street, with a torn lining she keeps her notes in
Pocket revolver, a .32 her editor made her take after the Herald's last reporter in the coalfields was put on a train with two broken fingers, 5 loaded, in her handbag
A press card from the Allegheny Labor Herald, a Pittsburgh weekly with nine thousand readers and two creditors
The anonymous letter, postmarked Gale, W. Va., 30 March 1927, in pencil on company-store wrapping paper
A folding Kodak camera with two rolls of film, and a flash lamp she has used twice
Three steno pads, six pencils and a penknife
A clipping file on the Ottway Smokeless Coal Company: the 1919 newspaper report of 'thirteen lost', the company's annual report, and a photograph of J. Rinehart Ottway at a Philadelphia charity ball
A return ticket to Pittsburgh by way of Huntington, good for thirty days
features: Seen It in a Book (Educated origin: once per long rest, recalls one true and useful fact of history, science, law or a book without a check; advantage on Research checks in a library, archive or registry; reads old handwriting and legal language without a check)

There's an Explanation (Skeptic: once per short rest, when she fails a fear check, she names a rational cause aloud, gas, a draught, settling rock, a prankster, and the failure becomes a success with no Dread; advantage on Investigation to find the mechanism behind anything that is a person's doing, and 10 minutes searching a room tells her whether any part of what is happening there is)

Careful Notes (Skeptic: once per short rest, after 10 minutes examining a scene, asks the GM 'What here has been moved?', 'Who was here most recently?' or 'What here does not fit?' and gets a true answer; it never names a creature's rule outright)

Calm Explanation (Skeptic, 2nd level: as an action, explains a frightening phenomenon to allies who can hear her; until the end of the scene they have advantage on fear checks against that one horror; once per long rest)

Discipline: Detective (Skeptic, 3rd level: advantage on Insight checks to tell whether a person is lying, and once per scenario a witness she has interviewed remembers one more true thing when she goes back to them)

The Morgue and the Wire (Reporter background: she can get into any newspaper's back files and its staff will help her, reads a court docket, a coroner's report and an inquest transcript, and finds the town gossip in any place with a paper; a story with her name on it tells everyone exactly who has been asking)

personality.traits: I write everything down, including what people say when they think I've stopped writing. I'm cheerful with company men because it confuses them. I believe in figures: tons, wages, prices at the store, the number of men on a list.
personality.ideals: A thing that is printed cannot be taken back. The company owns the houses, the store, the road and the sheriff; it does not own what nine thousand people read on Saturday.
personality.bonds: The man who wrote the letter, whoever he is. My editor, Sol Abramowitz, who has bet the paper's last libel insurance on this story. My father, who lost a hand at the Edgar Thomson works and never got a cent for it.
personality.flaws: I want the story so badly I forget it is happening to people. I will promise a source I'll keep their name out of it and then argue with myself all night about whether I have to.

appearance: A small, quick woman of twenty-nine with cropped dark hair under a cloche hat, a sharp freckled face, grey eyes that never quite stop moving, and ink on her right cuff. A man's coat too big for her, sensible shoes caked with Kettle Run mud by the end of the first day, a handbag heavier than it looks, and a camera on a strap.
backstory: Frances Lowry grew up in Braddock, Pennsylvania, in the smoke of the steel mills, the daughter of a crane man who lost his left hand in 1909 and a mother who took in washing. She got through the normal school on scholarships and taught third grade for one year, and then wrote a letter to the Allegheny Labor Herald about the company houses in Braddock that the editor printed on the front page, and she has been a reporter ever since. She has covered the steel strike of 1919 and the coal strikes in the northern fields, and she is good at it: she is small, polite and easy to underestimate, and she can add. On 4 April 1927 an envelope came to the Herald, postmarked Gale, West Virginia, with no name on it. Inside, in pencil on brown company-store paper: 'Ask the Ottway Smokeless Coal Company why its 1919 list says thirteen. Ask who capped the Number Two air shaft on the 17th of October and why. There is a man tapping behind the 7 North seal tonight and the company says it is the mountain settling. It is not. A friend of the men.' The Herald's files said the Ottway No. 3 explosion of 14 October 1919 killed thirteen men, that the fire was sealed in 'according to accepted practice', and that a guard at Ottway named Lester Gaither went missing on 25 March 1927 and two union men are in the Gale jail for his murder. Sol Abramowitz gave her forty dollars and a ticket. She has told the company, in writing, that she is coming to write a piece on 'the modern mining town'. She has not yet found out that the company already knows who she is.
